title: Neighbourhood Problem Spotter
goal: Your kid walks your neighbourhood with you and looks at it like a detective. They spot what could work better, pick one problem worth solving, find out why it's there, design the simplest fix that could work, and pitch it to someone who can say yes.
need: A place you can walk together: your street, a park, a campground or a market
Paper, a pencil and something to lean on

academics.subject: Geography
academics.text: drawing a map and reading patterns on it

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: You don't need to know anything about city planning. Your job is to be the walking partner: go slowly, take what they notice seriously and keep asking 'Who would have trouble here?' A kid's eye level catches things adults stopped seeing years ago.

plan.what: Walk, notice and map what you find (Steps 1 and 2).
Dig for evidence and design the fix (Steps 3 and 4).
Pitch it and do the part you can do (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Look for what's missing, not what's broken: no bench on the hill, no shade at the bus stop, nowhere for kids to meet.

troubleshoot.q: We live rurally, or we're travelling
troubleshoot.a: Use the closest shared place: the community hall, a trail, the campground, a market. Same steps, different map.
Shrink it. Not 'traffic', but 'nobody can see around this corner'. A small problem can get a real answer.

lesson.text: Most complaints stop at what's wrong. A proposal says where, who it affects, why it happens, what would help and who can say yes.
lesson.before: The park is always gross. Someone should clean it.

model.line: The bin by the playground gate, full on 3 of our 4 visits.
It's the only bin in the park, and it fills up on weekends.
A second bin near the picnic tables, or an extra pickup on Friday afternoon.
An email to the parks department, with our count.

lesson.modelNote: The first version is a grumble. The second has a count, a cause and a person to send it to.

steps.title: Walk and notice
steps.why: You walk past most of your neighbourhood without seeing it.
steps.kid: Your kid walks a loop with you, slowly, and looks for what works and what could work better, using the What to look for card in the Spotter Toolkit at the end of the guide. They jot or sketch each thing and where it was.
steps.you: Walk at their pace and let them stop. Add 'Who would have trouble here?' and try it from a stroller, a wheelchair or a very small kid's point of view.
ask: What do you walk past every day and never really look at?
Who would have the hardest time here?
steps.tip: Photograph places, not people or licence plates. Stay on public paths, and stay together.

levels.explore: Find two things that could be better and draw or describe each one.
levels.develop: Find three or four and sort them by type: safety, clean, access, nature, together.
levels.extend: Walk the same loop at night or in the rain, and compare what you find.

steps.title: Map it and pick one
steps.why: You can't solve everything. Picking is the first real decision.
steps.kid: Your kid draws a simple map with home, the main streets and a numbered mark for each thing they found. Then they use the Pick one card to choose the problem worth their time.
steps.you: Help with which way the streets run if they get stuck. Then keep your favourite to yourself. The problem has to be one they care about.
ask: Are the problems spread out or all in one spot?
Which one bothers you the most, and why?
steps.tip: Choose something a person could actually change. 'No crossing near the park' works. 'Winter is too long' doesn't.

levels.explore: Draw the route and mark your problems, then pick the one you care about most.
levels.develop: Colour-code the map by type, and compare three problems using the Pick one card.
levels.extend: Score every problem for how many people it affects and how doable it is, and defend the top choice.

steps.title: Dig for evidence
steps.why: A count and a photo get taken seriously. A feeling doesn't.
steps.kid: Your kid goes back and gathers evidence: a count, a few visits at different times, a photo. They talk to one or two people it affects, then keep asking why until they reach a cause, and use the Who looks after it card to find out whose job it is.
steps.you: Come along for every conversation with a neighbour or shop owner, and stand beside them while they ask. Help them find the right page on your town's website.
ask: What does your count tell you?
steps.tip: Go back at a different time of day. Lots of problems only show up at rush hour or after a weekend.

levels.explore: Come up with two reasons the problem might be happening.
levels.develop: Count it on three visits, ask one person about it, and name the cause and who looks after it.
levels.extend: Find a place that solved a similar problem and work out what they did differently.

steps.title: Design the simplest fix
steps.why: The fix that gets done beats the perfect one that doesn't.
steps.kid: Your kid comes up with at least two fixes, then picks the simplest one that could really work. They write down what it needs, who would have to agree and how long it would take, then fill in the Proposal page at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Ask 'How would that actually work?' Then play the other side: 'There's no money for this' or 'My neighbour likes it the way it is.' Let them answer.
ask: What would it cost, and who would pay?
Who might say no, and why?
steps.tip: Cheap and small gets a yes more often. A sign, a bin or a painted line is easier to agree to than a new park.

levels.explore: Draw your fix and say in a few sentences how it helps.
levels.develop: Fill in the Proposal page with what, who and how long, and answer one objection.
levels.extend: Compare two fixes for cost and effort, cost out the winner, and answer every objection you can think of.

steps.title: Pitch it and do your part
steps.why: An idea nobody hears doesn't change anything.
steps.kid: Your kid practises the 30-second pitch from the Pitch it card on the family, fixes the weak spots from your questions, then shares it with someone who can say yes. They also pick one small part of the problem they can take care of themselves this week.
steps.you: Be the tough but kind audience. Send or deliver anything that goes outside the family with them, and read it first. Then help with their small part.
ask: What can we do this week without asking anyone?
steps.tip: A short, polite email from a kid, with a count and a photo, tends to get read. An answer isn't guaranteed, and that's a real lesson too.

levels.explore: Tell the family the problem and your fix, then do one small thing to help.
levels.develop: Give the 30-second pitch, improve it, and share it with a neighbour or a local group.
levels.extend: Send your proposal to the person responsible, follow up after two weeks, and report back on what happened.

conclusion.headline: They'll never walk that street the same way again.
conclusion.text: Walk the same loop in a month. If they point at something and say 'Why is it like that?' or 'Who looks after that?', they've started to see their neighbourhood as something people make, and something they can have a say in.
conclusion.celebrate: Go back together to the spot it all started and do their small fix there. Then say: 'You noticed this. Most people just walk by.'
extensions: Do the same walk in a different neighbourhood and compare
Interview neighbours about what they'd love to see changed
Organize a clean-up or planting morning with a few families
Look for what works really well nearby and thank whoever looks after it

signs: They point out things that could work better on ordinary walks
They ask why something is the way it is, and whose job it is
They bring evidence when they want to change your mind
makeItReal: Keep the proposal somewhere visible and check back in a month: did anything change, and who should they follow up with?

onTheRoad: Spot one thing this place does better than home, like shade, benches, bins or crossings, and work out why it works.
Count how people get around here for ten minutes, walking, biking, buses or scooters, and compare it with your street.
Photograph three clever small fixes around town, like a sign, a ramp or a shared shelf, and guess who made each one.
backHome: Pick one fix you saw on the road, check whether it would help your own street, and pitch it to whoever looks after it.
